summary: Defines a Management Information Base (MIB) module for monitoring and managing the Virtual Fabrics function of Fibre Channel networks through network management protocols such as SNMP.

eli5.summary: A big storage network can be split into several pretend smaller networks. This note defines a standard list of dials and gauges so management software can look at and control those pretend networks.

subtitle: A standard set of SNMP objects for watching and configuring Virtual Fabrics in Fibre Channel switches.

tldr.problem: Fibre Channel lets one physical Fabric be split into several logical Virtual Fabrics, but network management software had no standard way to see or configure them.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 4747 defines the T11-FC-VIRTUAL-FABRIC-MIB module, four tables that describe Core Switches, Virtual Switches, per-port Virtual Fabric settings and locally enabled VF_IDs, built on top of the Fibre Channel Management MIB from RFC 4044.
tldr.outcome: Management tools can use SNMP to monitor Virtual Fabrics and, where an implementation allows it, to create Virtual Switches and set port tagging. The RFC is a Proposed Standard and is not marked as obsoleted or updated.

today: RFC 4747 is a Proposed Standard and the unit metadata lists no obsoleting or updating RFC. It builds on RFC 4044.

sections.title: What the Virtual Fabrics MIB Covers
sections.content:
RFC 4747 defines a portion of the Management Information Base (MIB) for the Fibre Channel network's Virtual Fabrics function. A MIB is a virtual information store of managed objects, which are generally accessed through the Simple Network Management Protocol (SNMP).

The module is written in SMIv2, the Structure of Management Information described in RFC 2578, RFC 2579 and RFC 2580. It lets a management client monitor Virtual Fabric functionality and configure some of its parameters. The MIB defines no "managed actions" that could be invoked remotely through SNMP.
sections.eli5: This note lists the standard questions a manager can ask a storage switch about its pretend sub-networks. It only asks and sets values; it does not push buttons that do things.

sections.title: Fibre Channel and Virtual Fabrics Background
sections.content:
Fibre Channel (FC) is logically a bidirectional point-to-point serial data channel that carries higher-level protocols such as SCSI command sets and IP. Nodes connect through N_Ports to a Fabric, a switching network. Many components have globally unique names, usually formatted as World Wide Names (WWNs), and frames carry 24-bit address identifiers.

Virtual Fabrics allow one physical Fabric to be divided into multiple logical Fabrics. Each can be managed independently like a traditional Fabric. The stated goals are better use of the physical infrastructure and isolation of events in one Virtual Fabric from the others.

When one Core Switch provides switching for several Virtual Fabrics, it is modeled as containing several Virtual Switches, one per Virtual Fabric. Each Virtual Fabric has a 12-bit Virtual Fabric ID (VF_ID). On a shared physical link, the VF_ID in a frame's Virtual Fabric Tagging Header says which Virtual Fabric the frame belongs to, and tagging is enabled through an initial negotiation between the two connected ports.
sections.eli5: One big switch pretends to be several smaller ones. Each pretend switch has a number on its name tag, and traffic on a shared cable carries that number so it goes to the right one.

sections.title: How the MIB Fits with RFC 4044
sections.content:
This MIB extends the Fibre Channel Management MIB (RFC 4044). A Fibre Channel management instance is a separable managed instance of Fibre Channel functionality, and the object fcmInstanceIndex identifies each one. The text gives the example of one SNMP agent with several AgentX sub-agents, each implementing a different instance.

When Virtual Switches exist, the fcmSwitchTable from RFC 4044 contains a row for each Virtual Switch. The new t11vfCoreSwitchTable and t11vfVirtualSwitchTable are complementary to it and help a manager tell which switches are virtual and how each relates to a Core Switch. A Virtual Switch must reside in a single Core Switch, and a Core Switch is a set of entities with the same Core Switch_Name.

RFC 4044 predates standard Virtual Switches and did not define its tables as read-create. Because administrators can now create Virtual Switches, this MIB adds read-create behavior, and its StorageTypes should also apply to the RFC 4044 tables it augments.
sections.eli5: An older list already described the real switches. This new list adds extra columns for the pretend ones and lets managers add new pretend switches.

sections.title: The Tables in the Module
sections.content:
The module is T11-FC-VIRTUAL-FABRIC-MIB, assigned number 147 under mib-2. It has four tables.

  • t11vfCoreSwitchTable: one row per Core Switch, indexed by fcmInstanceIndex and the Core Switch_Name. Its t11vfCoreSwitchMaxSupported is 1 on switches without Virtual Fabrics, or the maximum number of Virtual Fabrics otherwise (range 1 to 4095, ignoring the Control VF_ID).
  • t11vfVirtualSwitchTable: one row per Virtual Switch, augmenting fcmSwitchTable one-to-one. It holds the VF_ID the switch serves, the name of its Core Switch, and a RowStatus so a Virtual Switch can be created remotely. Creating or deleting a row also creates or deletes the matching fcmSwitchTable row.
  • t11vfPortTable: augments fcmPortEntry with a Port VF_ID (the default Virtual Fabric for untagged frames, default 1), tagging admin status, tagging operational status and a storage type.
  • t11vfLocallyEnabledTable: one row per locally enabled VF_ID on each port, indexed by interface index and VF_ID, with an operational status, row status and storage type.

Every table also carries a StorageType column with a default of nonVolatile.
sections.eli5: There are four lists: one for the big switches, one for the pretend switches, one for each cable socket, and one saying which pretend networks may use each socket.

sections.title: Port Tagging and Locally Enabled Fabrics
sections.content:
Tagging is controlled per port by t11vfPortTaggingAdminStatus, which can be set to three values.

  • off(1) disables Virtual Fabric tagging on the port.
  • on(2) enables tagging if the attached port does not prohibit it.
  • auto(3) enables tagging if the peer requests it.

The read-only t11vfPortTaggingOperStatus reports whether tagging is actually off(1) or on(2).

The set of Virtual Fabrics operational on a port is the bit-wise AND of the port's locally enabled VF_IDs and those of the attached port. Rows in the locally enabled table cannot be modified while active, except for the row status and storage type objects. The Control VF_ID is implicitly enabled and is not set, and communication with it is required.
sections.eli5: A cable socket can be told always to use name tags, never, or only when the other end asks. Two ends can only share the pretend networks that both of them allow.

sections.title: Conformance Requirements
sections.content:
Compliance requires the mandatory group t11vfGeneralGroup, which collects all the objects for monitoring and configuring Virtual Fabrics in a Fibre Channel switch. The compliance statement relaxes write access: t11vfCoreSwitchMaxSupported, the VF_ID, storage type and tagging admin objects, and the row status objects (restricted to active(1)) may all be implemented as read-only.

So a compliant switch need not let managers change its Virtual Fabric configuration over SNMP. It must at least report it.
sections.eli5: A switch has to be able to answer the questions. It is allowed to refuse to let managers change the answers.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Objects with a MAX-ACCESS of read-write or read-create can be sensitive. Changing them can alter the configuration of Virtual Fabrics on a switch (for example t11vfCoreSwitchMaxSupported, t11vfVirtualSwitchVfId and t11vfVirtualSwitchRowStatus) or on a port (for example t11vfPortTaggingAdminStatus and t11vfPortVfId). Some readable objects, such as t11vfVirtualSwitchCoreSwitchName and the two operational status objects, reveal how Virtual Fabrics are configured.

SNMP versions before SNMPv3 did not include adequate security. The RFC says deploying them is NOT RECOMMENDED, and RECOMMENDS SNMPv3 with cryptographic security. Operators must make sure only principals with legitimate rights can GET or SET the objects. IANA assigned 147 for the module under the appropriate subtree.
sections.eli5: Anyone who can change these settings could mess up the pretend networks, so only trusted people should get to, and the messages should be protected.

items.title: Core Switch table
items.text: One row per Core Switch, with the maximum number of Virtual Fabrics it supports.

items.title: Virtual Switch table
items.text: One row per Virtual Switch; rows can be created remotely.

items.title: Port table
items.text: Port VF_ID and tagging status added to each Fibre Channel port.

items.title: Locally Enabled table
items.text: Which VF_IDs are enabled on each port.
